title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: In banking, your raw material is deposits, your factory is your technology stack, and your distribution is trust—if you overpay for deposits, the rest of the P&L never recovers.
epigraph.author: Commercial Banking Primer

web_blocks.html: A universal bank's 'supply chain' is its funding architecture—how it gathers, prices, and retains customer deposits. Its 'distribution' is the omni-channel network that originates loans, processes payments, and distributes wealth products. JPMorgan Chase's structural cost edge starts with deposit gathering. Chase operates over 5,000 physical branches across all 48 contiguous U.S. states [10]. It also plans to open 160+ new branches and renovate nearly 600 locations through 2026 [10]. Paired with the nation's #1 mobile banking app (~75 million digitally active users), Chase wins primary household checking accounts at far lower funding costs than online banks or regional peers [10].

Why do physical branches still matter in a digital era? Over 41 million customers visit a Chase branch each year [10]. Branches act as high-trust acquisition anchors for Chase Private Client wealth, small-business treasury, mortgages, and auto loans [10]. Once a household sets up direct deposit and bill pay in the Chase app, switching costs rise sharply. That keeps deposit betas far below institutional money market funds. On the wholesale side, J.P. Morgan Payments embeds directly into corporate ERP systems via APIs. It handles global cash concentration, FX, and merchant acquiring—generating sticky, non-interest-bearing operating deposits for CIB.

Three unit-economic levers govern JPMorgan's cost structure. First is compensation and technology: $54.49B of compensation sits inside $95.64B of FY2025 noninterest expense across ~318,512 employees, alongside ~$17B+ in annual tech/AI spend [1, 20]. Second is credit provisioning: FY2025 provision for credit losses totaled $14.21B to cover normalized card charge-offs and CECL reserves [1]. Third is capital intensity: JPM holds a 13.9%–14.6% CET1 buffer against risk-weighted assets [1, 3]. Spreading fixed tech and compliance costs across $182.45B of revenue keeps its efficiency ratio near ~52.4% [1].

web_blocks.caption: FY2025 Audited Net Revenue-to-Net Income Waterfall ($M, GAAP Basis; $100 Unit-Economics Scaling)
web_blocks.takeaway: Out of every $100 of FY2025 GAAP net revenue ($182,447M), JPMorgan Chase spent $29.86 on employee compensation ($54,487M), $30.35 on non-compensation operating expenses plus credit loss provisions ($41,153M non-comp opex + $14,212M PCL = $55,365M), and $8.52 on income taxes ($15,547M)—converting $31.27 per $100 into net income ($57,048M). Note: unlike industrial firms, bank distributable capital equals net income less CET1 capital retained for RWA growth (~30%–40% of net income).

web_blocks.html: That 31.3% net profit margin ($31.27 of net income per $100 of net revenue) is extraordinary in global banking [1]. Notice how the unit economics hold together even as interest rates normalize: in Q3 2026, managed net revenue rose 8% year-over-year to $50.9 billion, while total NII climbed 13% to $27.1 billion (and NII ex-Markets rose 6% to $24.7 billion), absorbing $2.7 billion in quarterly credit costs ($2.2B net charge-offs + $539M reserve build) to still print $15.3 billion in quarterly net income [3].

Beyond deposit beta and overhead leverage, JPMorgan's card and merchant ecosystem illustrates how customer acquisition cost (CAC) and lifetime value (LTV) compound at national scale. Co-branded and proprietary card programs—led by Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, Freedom, Ink Business, and the newly contracted Apple Card forward purchase commitment—require upfront rewards and marketing investment, but once embedded in a household's digital wallet, generate recurring interchange fees, annual fees, and high-yield revolving balances [1, 11]. Meanwhile, AI-driven fraud detection and automated underwriting lower unit servicing costs per account even as total card volumes expand.

On the institutional side, J.P. Morgan Payments processes trillions of dollars in daily wholesale clearing, FX, and merchant acquiring [13]. Corporate treasurers embed Chase APIs straight into ERP and payroll systems. Client churn stays minimal, and operating deposits carry near-zero rate sensitivity. Together, retail checking, Sapphire cards, and treasury APIs form a three-tier funding flywheel. That keeps net revenue per asset dollar structurally higher than regional peers.

Deposit beta discipline is the core of this unit-economic edge. When rates surged in 2022–2023, online-only banks had to pay near-Fed-funds rates to retain deposits. Chase held onto trillions in primary checking balances at far lower cost. Across a $2.4 trillion deposit base, even a 100 bps funding advantage generates $24 billion in annual spread before a single loan is written.

That funding edge also lowers credit risk. Banks with expensive deposits are forced to chase riskier, higher-yielding loans just to earn a spread. Because JPMorgan's funding cost is structurally low, it can underwrite prime consumers and investment-grade corporations while still earning a 20% ROTCE [1]. Low-cost deposits and conservative credit underwriting reinforce each other.

book_paragraphs: If you want to know whether a bank is genuinely great or merely lucky with interest rates, ignore its marketing slogans and look at its supply chain. Wait—a bank has a supply chain? Absolutely. Every bank is a spread-and-fee factory whose raw material is money. If you gather your raw material—deposits—by paying 4.5% on promotional CDs to hot-money rate shoppers, you are buying expensive steel and trying to sell cheap cars. You will eventually get squeezed. JPMorgan Chase's secret weapon is that it gathers its raw material at the lowest structural cost in American banking.

How does it pull that off? Through a two-pronged distribution machine that rivals have spent billions trying to imitate. First is the physical-plus-digital consumer flywheel. Chase operates over 5,000 branches across all lower 48 states—and remarkably, while competitors have been shuttering branches to save rent, Chase has been opening 160+ new locations and renovating nearly 600 more. Why? Because 41 million Americans still walk into a Chase branch every year, and branches act as trust anchors that convert casual savers into Chase Private Client wealth relationships and small-business accounts. Pair that physical footprint with 75 million digitally active users on the #1 mobile banking app in the country, and you create frictionless stickiness. Once your paycheck, mortgage, and Sapphire card live inside one app, you do not move your checking account for an extra 50 basis points down the street.

Second is the institutional plumbing inside J.P. Morgan Payments. When multinational corporations plug their global treasury and payroll into JPMorgan's APIs, they park billions of dollars in operating checking balances—not to chase yield, but because those balances clear their daily invoices. That gives JPMorgan a massive cushion of sticky, low-beta funding.

Now let us walk through the $100 bill test on JPMorgan's audited FY2025 income statement so you can see the unit economics with crystal clarity. Out of every $100 of net revenue ($182.45 billion total), JPMorgan paid $29.86 to its 318,512 employees in compensation and benefits ($54.49 billion). It spent another $22.56 on non-compensation operating costs—branches, data centers, $17B+ of technology and AI engineering, and marketing—and set aside $7.79 for credit loss provisions ($14.21 billion) to cover normalizing card and commercial charge-offs. After paying $8.52 to the taxman ($15.55 billion), an astonishing $31.27 out of every $100 dropped straight to the bottom line as net income ($57.05 billion). That is why scale matters in modern banking: JPMorgan spreads a $17 billion technology budget over a $182 billion revenue base, a math equation no regional bank can match.

Think about what that $31.27 net margin means in practical terms. Even when credit card losses normalize and JPMorgan puts $2.7 billion a quarter into credit costs—as it did in Q3 2026—the bank still generates $15.3 billion in quarterly net income. And look at the unit economics of its Chase card ecosystem: acquiring a Sapphire or Ink Business customer costs real money upfront in sign-up bonuses and marketing, yet once that card becomes the default payment method in Apple Pay or a small business's expense ledger, Chase earns interchange on every swipe for years while cross-selling checking, auto loans, and wealth management at near-zero incremental acquisition cost.

That is the difference between a commodity lender and a financial platform. A regional bank has to pay up for deposits and buy loan participations just to keep its assets growing. JPMorgan owns the customer relationship at the front door—both the household checking account and the corporate treasury API—which gives it structural pricing power on both sides of the balance sheet.

book_subsections.title: The Hidden Economics of Deposit Beta and Technology Amortization
paragraphs: If you want to sound like a seasoned bank analyst at dinner, ask one question about any bank: 'What is its through-the-cycle deposit beta?' Deposit beta simply measures how much of a Federal Reserve rate hike a bank has to pass along to its depositors. When rates jumped by 500 basis points in 2022 and 2023, online-only banks and weak regional lenders had to pay 4.5% to 5.0% just to stop money from walking out the door—a deposit beta approaching 80% or 90%.

JPMorgan Chase's deposit beta stayed dramatically lower because its customers hold checking accounts for convenience, payroll direct deposit, Zelle payments, and Sapphire rewards—not to squeeze out an extra half-percent of yield. Multiply that 100 to 200 basis points of funding cost advantage across more than $2 trillion of deposits, and you are looking at tens of billions of dollars in structural annual spread advantage before the bank even makes a single loan.

Now pair that cheap funding with technology amortization. Spending $17 billion a year on software engineers, cloud data centers, and AI fraud models would bankrupt a $10 billion regional bank. Spread across JPMorgan's $182.45 billion net revenue base, however, it keeps the overhead efficiency ratio near 52% while making the mobile app faster and safer every quarter—pulling in yet more primary checking accounts and widening the lead.

book_subsections.title: The Card & Payments Flywheel: How CAC Turns Into Decades of LTV
paragraphs: Think about how a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Chase Ink Business card actually makes money over ten years. In Year 1, Chase pays an upfront welcome bonus and marketing cost to put that card in a household's wallet. If a customer cancels in Month 13, Chase loses money. Yet Chase's retention is extraordinarily high because the card is wired directly into the Chase mobile app, Ultimate Rewards travel portal, and primary checking relationship.

Once a family uses that card for groceries, flights, and gas—especially after the 2026 Sapphire Preferred enhancements—Chase collects recurring interchange fees on every swipe, annual fee revenue, and high-margin revolving interest from balances carried over time. Meanwhile, on the corporate side, J.P. Morgan Payments locks in global treasurers with API-driven cash management and FX settlement, creating a two-sided payments moat that compounds year after year.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The $100 revenue waterfall reveals JPMorgan Chase's true operating leverage: even after paying top-decile Wall Street and tech talent (~$30 per $100) and reserving conservatively for credit losses (~$8 per $100), over $31 of every $100 in net revenue converts into net profit.
bullets: Branch + App Hybrid: 5,000+ physical branches feed 75M+ digital users, keeping retail deposit betas structurally low.
Technology Scale: Only a $180B+ revenue bank can spend $17B+ annually on AI, cloud, and cybersecurity while maintaining a ~52% efficiency ratio.
